title: Deadlock Detection & Recovery
summary: Let deadlock happen, then find it and break it — the strategy real databases actually use, since preventing every deadlock structurally is often more expensive than occasionally cleaning one up.

slides.markdown:
Prevention and avoidance both try to stop deadlock from ever happening. **Detection and recovery** takes a different bet entirely: let the system run freely, allow deadlock to actually occur, periodically check whether it has, and if so, forcibly break it.

This sounds reckless, but it's exactly what production databases do with transaction deadlocks — and for good reason, covered on the last slide. This topic covers how detection actually works and the two real recovery strategies once a deadlock is confirmed.

slides.sectionTitle: Why some systems allow deadlock and detect it instead of avoiding it
slides.markdown:
Prevention and avoidance both pay a cost on the **common, non-deadlocking path** — lock ordering constrains how code is written everywhere, and avoidance's safety check runs on every single resource request, whether or not deadlock was ever actually going to happen. Detection flips that trade: pay nothing on the common path, and pay a real cost only on the rare occasions deadlock actually occurs.

This is the right trade specifically when deadlocks are genuinely rare relative to total operations, and when there's an acceptable way to recover once one is found — both of which are true for database transactions: a deadlock between two transactions happens far less often than the millions of transactions that complete cleanly, and "abort one transaction and let the client retry" is a normal, acceptable outcome that database clients already expect to handle.

slides.sectionTitle: The detection algorithm: reducing the resource allocation graph
slides.markdown:
Detection reuses the same core idea as the Banker's Algorithm's safety check, run *after the fact* on the system's actual current state rather than *before* granting a hypothetical request: repeatedly find a process whose outstanding requests can be satisfied by currently available resources, pretend it finishes and releases everything, add that back to available, and repeat.

If every process eventually gets marked as able to finish, there's no deadlock — the graph fully **reduces**. If the process runs out of candidates while some processes are still stuck holding resources and unable to get what they need, those remaining unreduced processes are exactly the ones involved in an actual, confirmed deadlock — not just a theoretical risk, a real one, right now.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: wait-for graph and detecting a cycle
slides.markdown:
![Wait-for graph with a deadlock cycle](assets/wait-for-graph.svg)

A **wait-for graph** simplifies the resource allocation graph by removing resource nodes entirely and drawing a direct edge from a waiting process straight to the process holding what it wants — a cycle in this simpler graph means deadlock exactly the same way a resource allocation graph cycle does for single-instance resources. Note P4 here isn't part of the cycle even though it's waiting on P2 — it's just delayed, not deadlocked, since P2 isn't waiting on P4.

slides.sectionTitle: When to run detection — the frequency trade-off
slides.markdown:
Running the detection algorithm has a real cost — it's not free just because it runs "after the fact" instead of on every request. Run it too rarely, and processes stay needlessly deadlocked for a long time before anyone notices and recovers them, wasting whatever resources they hold. Run it too frequently (say, on every single resource request, checking the whole system state each time), and you've essentially recreated avoidance's per-request overhead without avoidance's guarantee of never actually deadlocking.

Real systems pick a middle ground based on the actual cost of staying deadlocked: databases typically run detection on a short fixed interval (fractions of a second to a few seconds) or trigger it specifically when a transaction has been waiting unusually long, rather than on a fixed universal schedule — tuning detection frequency to "how bad is it if a deadlock sits undetected for N seconds" for that specific system.

slides.sectionTitle: Recovery by process termination: one victim vs all
slides.markdown:
The simplest recovery once a deadlock is confirmed: kill one or more of the processes in the cycle, forcing it to release everything it holds and breaking the cycle for everyone else.

**Kill all deadlocked processes**: guaranteed to break the deadlock completely and immediately, but wastes all the work every one of them had done — often far more than necessary. **Kill one victim at a time, then re-check**: pick a single process from the cycle (based on some cost criterion — how much work it's done, how many resources it holds, its priority), terminate it, and re-run detection; if the deadlock is resolved, stop, otherwise pick another victim. This is far more conservative about wasted work but requires re-running detection after each termination, since killing one process doesn't always break every deadlock (some multi-cycle situations need more than one victim).

slides.sectionTitle: Recovery by resource preemption: rollback and victim selection
slides.markdown:
A less destructive alternative to killing a process outright: forcibly **preempt** one or more of the resources a deadlocked process holds (take them away without terminating the process), give them to another process in the cycle so it can proceed, and roll the preempted process back to a point before it acquired that resource so it can retry later.

This is exactly what production databases actually do for transaction deadlocks: instead of literally killing a process, the database **rolls back one transaction** (undoing its uncommitted changes cleanly, since transactions are designed to be rollback-safe) rather than the whole connection or application process — the client typically sees a "deadlock detected, transaction rolled back" error and is expected to retry. This works specifically because transactions are already built with rollback as a first-class, safe operation — that's the actual property that makes rollback-based recovery practical here, not something specific to databases in general.

slides.sectionTitle: The starvation risk of always picking the same victim
slides.markdown:
If victim selection always uses the same simple criterion — say, "always roll back the transaction with the lowest priority" or "always kill the most recently started process" — a specific process can end up being selected as the victim **repeatedly**, every time it re-enters a deadlock, and never actually complete. That's starvation, introduced by the recovery mechanism itself rather than by scheduling.

The standard fix mirrors how schedulers avoid starvation in general: factor the **number of times a process has already been rolled back** into victim selection, so a process that's already been a victim several times becomes progressively less likely to be picked again, guaranteeing it eventually gets to run to completion. Real databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL/InnoDB) implement exactly this kind of weighting in their deadlock victim-selection logic.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: detection+recovery vs avoidance vs prevention — which real systems use which
slides.markdown:
| | Prevention | Avoidance | Detection + recovery |
|---|---|---|---|
| When deadlock is stopped | Never possible at all | Never allowed to occur | Allowed to occur, then fixed |
| Common-path cost | Near zero (a coding discipline) | Real, on every request | Near zero, except when detection runs |
| Requires advance knowledge? | No | Yes (max resource needs) | No |
| Real-world examples | Lock ordering in application code, kernel `lockdep` | Rare — embedded/fixed-resource systems | Database transaction managers (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server) |

**How to decide:** prevention for code you control where a structural rule is enforceable. Detection+recovery for systems where deadlocks are rare, recovery is cheap and safe (rollback-capable transactions), and the alternative (avoidance's upfront-max requirement) doesn't fit the workload. Avoidance mainly where resource needs really are known in advance.

slides.sectionTitle: Why databases choose detection over prevention or avoidance
slides.markdown:
This is worth stating as a single, staff-level line, since it's the most commonly asked practical question in this whole group: databases can't easily use prevention (globally ordering every possible row lock across arbitrary application queries isn't practical — you don't control the order application code issues its SQL in), and they can't use avoidance (a transaction rarely knows every row it will ever touch before it starts, so declaring a Max upfront is unrealistic).

What they *do* have is a cheap, safe recovery mechanism already built into their core design: transactions are rollback-safe by construction, since atomicity requires the ability to undo a transaction's effects cleanly at any point before commit. That single property is what makes detection-and-recovery not just tolerable but genuinely the best fit — the "expensive" part of this strategy (recovery) is actually nearly free here, which flips the whole cost-benefit calculation compared to a system without safe rollback.
